blocks.text: HarborWorks can build a report dataset correctly, but returning it or placing it in a container appears to require repeated allocation and copying. Move semantics offer a different operation: transfer an existing resource when the source is no longer required to retain its old value. The benefit is not a mysterious faster copy. The benefit comes from changing what must be preserved.

blocks.text: The source still exists after a move unless its lifetime has separately ended. It must remain usable according to its documented post-move contract. This chapter gives its custom buffer a precise empty state so the transfer can be traced and tested. Standard-library types and user-defined types do not all promise the same visible post-move values.

topics.title: 5.1 Understanding Lvalues and Rvalues
topics.summary: Value categories describe expressions and influence overload selection. An lvalue commonly identifies an existing object whose identity can be used; prvalues and xvalues participate in the broader rvalue category. An object’s type and an expression’s value category are related but separate questions.

blocks.text: Lvalues are useful for identifying objects that can be accessed again. Passing a report lvalue to a by-value parameter normally preserves the caller’s report by copying, provided the type is copyable. A noncopyable owner rejects that path. This is useful feedback: the call site has not yet said that surrendering the resource is allowed.

blocks.text: Do not interpret “lvalue” as “stored on the stack” or “mutable.” A const object can be named by an lvalue expression. A dynamically allocated object can be accessed through an lvalue expression after dereferencing its pointer. Storage duration, const qualification, and value category are separate aspects of the language. Mixing them produces explanations that work for one tiny example and fail immediately in a real function.

blocks.text: The custom buffer has coupled members: its size describes the allocation owned by its unique pointer. Moving only the pointer would leave the source with a nonzero size and no storage. Its at method could then accept an index and attempt to access absent storage. The move constructor therefore transfers the pointer and exchanges the source’s size with zero as part of establishing the chosen empty-state contract.

blocks.text: A useful move-construction test records the source’s values, moves into a new buffer, and verifies the destination. It then checks that the source is empty and rejects checked access. Finally it assigns a new buffer to the source and uses it again. That last step distinguishes a valid reusable moved-from object from an object the test simply avoids touching until destruction.

This promise can affect container strategies for relocating elements; do not add noexcept to an operation that may actually propagate an exception, since an escaping exception would terminate the program.

Move assignment has two resources to consider: the source’s resource to acquire and the destination’s old resource to release. The unique pointer member handles release of the destination’s previous allocation when it receives the new ownership. The size member must then reflect the new representation, and the source must be put into the class’s documented empty state.

Self-move is a special case because source and destination are the same object. The teaching buffer explicitly checks this and leaves itself unchanged. That is its chosen contract, not a claim that every standard-library type preserves the same value after self-move assignment. For an unfamiliar type, consult the actual operation requirements and avoid depending on an unstated value guarantee.

Think about failure before calling a consuming function. If the caller writes accept(std::move(report)), construction of the receiving parameter may already transfer the caller’s state before accept validates a business rule. A later error result does not undo that transfer automatically. A preservation requirement may require inspection before transfer, a copy of the accepted state, or a staged candidate owned separately from the caller’s current value.

Move assignment should be reviewed alongside destruction, copying, and move construction. Declaring one special member can affect which others are generated. A design that was copy-only does not acquire efficient moves simply because a call site begins using std::move; overload resolution may still select a copy or reject the expression.

blocks.text: The standard library generally specifies valid but unspecified states for moved-from objects unless a particular operation provides a more specific guarantee. “Valid” means the object’s invariants are preserved and operations can be used when their preconditions are satisfied. “Unspecified” means the caller should not guess the retained value from one implementation’s behavior.

paragraphs: A defaulted move operation can be wrong for a representation with redundant or coupled state. If one member owns storage and another independently records its length, moving the owner and copying the scalar may leave the source’s invariant broken. The fix is either a custom move that repairs the relationship or a simpler representation whose size is derived from the owning member.

topics.title: Review and solution reasoning
topics.summary: A named rvalue-reference variable is still an lvalue expression. A cast does not itself transfer a resource. A custom buffer must preserve its size/storage invariant in both source and destination. Nothrow moves can help container operations, but a false noexcept promise makes failure less recoverable rather than making the code faster by definition.
